source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (matrix reasoning)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) beat UCLA undergraduates zero-shot on text Digit Matrices built like Raven's matrices. Its difficulty profile matched humans: progression rules and spatial permutation hurt both.
numbers: Humans N=40. Generative: odds ratio 1.88 for GPT-3 vs humans (p=0.005, CI 1.21-2.91). Multiple choice: OR 6.27 (p=2.3e-8). Per-subtype correlation GPT-3 vs human r(30)=0.39, p=0.027. Best human got every item right.
limits: Synthetic digit rules, not natural relations. Later work (c05 to c08) shows brittleness to altered problems.
agent_relevance: Pattern induction by relation is within LLM reach on familiar formats, but a mapping scored by code should not assume it holds under changed surface form.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (letter strings)
finding: GPT-3 solved letter-string analogies at or above average human level on most of six transformation types and on generalisation variants; GPT-4 preliminary tests were better.
numbers: Humans N=57 (letter strings). Correlation of GPT-3 vs human accuracy across problem types: r=0.6 (prompt format) and r=0.76 (sentence format), n=40 types.
limits: Alphabets were the standard Roman alphabet, likely in training data. Hodel and West (c05) and Lewis and Mitchell (c07) test this.
agent_relevance: Letter strings are a source-to-target rule transfer, a thin version of mapping. Useful as a cheap regression test for O7, not as proof of relational mapping.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (story analogies, Gentner materials)
finding: On Gentner's story-analogy materials, where the right target shares causal (higher-order) relations with the source and the foil shares only first-order relations, GPT-3 picked the causal match in near analogy but not reliably in far analogy. Students clearly beat GPT-3 here.
numbers: Humans N=54; 15 of 54 picked the analogous story on every trial. Combined near and far: GPT-3 binomial p=0.0005. Near: GPT-3 p=0.0039. Far: GPT-3 p=0.065 (not significant); humans t(53)=16.7. GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=0.0003. GPT-4 informally stronger, near ceiling in near analogy.
limits: GPT-4 result is supplementary and not a full study. Later paper (c08) finds order and paraphrase effects.
agent_relevance: This is the closest LLM test of the systematicity claim (prefer causal systems over shared surface relations). Far analogy is where an unaided model is weakest, so O7 needs an explicit relation-system check there.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (four-term verbal analogies)
finding: On four-term verbal analogies GPT-3 performed at or above student level, with a similar pattern across relation types (categorical, compositional, causal).
numbers: Humans N=57 on verbal analogies; chance 20 percent in the multiple-choice version. Relation-type breakdown is in the paper's Fig. 7 (values not extracted).
limits: Word analogies need only one relation, so systematicity is not tested.
agent_relevance: Single-relation mapping is easy for models; the hard part for the agent is multi-relation systems.

source: Hodel and West (2023) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed generalisation of Webb et al. Modified letter-string problems (permuted or synthetic alphabets, same rules) collapsed GPT-3 while humans stayed flat. They argue the original success may reflect training exposure to the standard alphabet.
numbers: Humans were consistently more accurate than GPT-3 on modified problems. GPT-3 generative accuracy on the synthetic alphabet was below 0.1 for extend sequence, successor/predecessor and fix alphabetic sequence. A comprehension check showed GPT-3 could still process the altered alphabet at at least 30 percent of the original level. 50 instances per type.
limits: Only GPT-3 tested. Webb et al. replied (c06) that GPT-4 with code execution closes the gap.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: a model's apparent mapping skill can be surface recall. Test O7 on altered (counterfactual) cases.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Reply to critics. GPT-4 alone fell below humans on counterfactual letter strings, but GPT-4 with code execution (self-written code to convert letters to indices) matched human level. Errors then looked humanlike.
numbers: GPT-4 vs humans: P=8.9e-13 (humans better). GPT-4 + code execution vs humans: P=0.496 (no difference). 46 percent of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39 percent in human errors reported by Lewis and Mitchell. 300 interval-1 problems run for GPT-4. Code use was not instructed.
limits: The fix is an external tool for counting, which supports a tool-use rather than a pure language account.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the schema idea that code checks help: letting the model offload the symbolic part to code restored human-level performance. Matches O7 scored by code.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Letter-string analogies with permuted alphabets or symbols: human accuracy stayed high, all three GPT models dropped as the alphabet got more scrambled. GPT-4 was no better than GPT-3 overall. Error types differ: humans used alternative valid rules (38.6 percent of errors), GPT-3 mostly wrong or copy errors.
numbers: Overall accuracy (table text-extracted, label alignment inferred): humans 0.753, GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452. Humans N=1,876 trials; 6,840 per GPT model. Error shares (alternative / literal / wrong / other): GPT-3 5.8/31.0/55.5/7.7 percent; GPT-4 22.0/32.7/42.7/2.7; humans 38.6/14.7/34.2/12.5.
limits: Table layout was garbled in text extraction; check the PDF before quoting per-model figures. Authors guess chat tuning may hurt.
agent_relevance: Report generalisation under altered surface, not just baseline accuracy, when judging any mapping step.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Extended robustness tests to three of Webb's four domains. Letter strings: humans steady, GPT models drop. Digit matrices: drop on only one of two variant types. Story analogies: GPT models showed answer-order effects and more paraphrase sensitivity than humans.
numbers: Two variant types per domain. No percentages on the abstract page (full paper not read).
limits: Only the abstract page was read this session.
agent_relevance: For O7, shuffle the order of candidate analogues and paraphrase them; if the choice flips, the mapping is not trustworthy.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière, Pavlick (2024) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning
finding: Humans and several LLMs (GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Llama-405B and others) did mapping between meaningful words and letter strings across about 13 conditions. Best models matched humans in the default condition but fell much more when distractors, order permutations or right-hand-side-only formats were added.
numbers: Human cells were small, about 15 to 18 per condition (Defaults 18, Distracted 18, Permuted Pairs 17, Random Finals 15). In Defaults GPT-4, Claude 3 and Llama-405B were not different from humans by logistic regression; Claude 3 and GPT-4 then dropped much more than humans under distractor-type conditions.
limits: Exact per-condition accuracies were not cleanly extracted from the PDF text. Numbers above are from methods and results prose only.
agent_relevance: Models match on easy cases, not under distractors. Distractor-heavy mapping tests are the right check for O7.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis, Chai (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Encoding visual Raven matrices as language lets pre-trained models solve them zero-shot. More abstraction (naming attributes, then decomposing the task into independent sub-problems) raised accuracy, and smaller models gained most from decomposition.
numbers: GPT-3 175B on the Center sub-task: 77.2 percent with naming, 80.0 percent with decomposition. With full decomposition, 87.8 percent on 2x2Grid and 93.2 percent on 3x3Grid, above human level on those. Component decomposition alone raised maximum accuracy by about 20 percent on average. 500 test items per RAVEN sub-task.
limits: Task is rule induction over attribute grids; mapping is trivial once attributes are named. Authors note decomposition may do part of the reasoning.
agent_relevance: The gain came from handing the model a pre-built relational description. This is the same move as typing the cases for O7 before mapping.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (analogical prompting)
finding: Asking the model to recall relevant solved problems before solving improved on 0-shot and 0-shot chain of thought, with an average accuracy gain of about 4 percent, and matched or beat few-shot CoT without labelled examples.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5-turbo: 5-shot CoT 75.0 percent vs self-generated exemplars 75.8 percent. MATH: 33.0 vs 33.9 percent (table rows partly garbled in extraction). Exemplars: K=5 for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH and BIG-Bench. Also Codeforces, where self-generated knowledge helped. Self-consistency adds further gains.
limits: Gain is not clearly due to analogy. Later work (c12) argues otherwise. Table rows were partly garbled.
agent_relevance: The only structure-mapping-flavoured method already inside an LLM loop at scale, but it retrieves by recall with no mapping step, so it is O7 without the mapping.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Relevant or random: can LLMs truly perform analogical reasoning?
finding: Self-generated relevant exemplars did not beat irrelevant ones. What mattered was whether the generated exemplars were correct. Random biology examples gave a gain over relevant ones on GSM8K.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo GSM8K: relevant 71.5, none 75.5, random-same-task 75.1, random-different-task 76.3, random-bio 75.3. MATH: relevant 33.3, none 36.1, random-same 36.3. BBH average of 5 tasks: relevant 63.2, none 61.9. Manual check of 50 samples per type: exemplars correct 62 percent for relevant, 72 for none, 86 for random-same. Llama-3-8B GSM8K relevant 69.5 vs random-diff 74.1; GPT-4o-mini relevant 90.7 vs random-bio 93.2.
limits: Math tasks mainly. Relevance helped only on BBH. The key factor named is exemplar accuracy, so a verifier on the exemplar may be what matters. Author list not verified.
agent_relevance: Evidence against unverified self-generated analogues (agrees with SCHEMA claim that unaided analogy rarely transfers). Check an analogue before mapping to it.

source: StoryAnalogy: deriving story-level analogies from LLMs (2023)
finding: 24,388 story pairs annotated for entity and relation similarity (from extended structure-mapping theory). Models, even large ones, fall far below humans at picking the analogous story; fine-tuning a smaller encoder did better than prompting a large model.
numbers: Identification, 4-way multiple choice: humans 85.7 percent, chance 25 percent, best LLM (FlanT5-xxl 1-shot) 46.3, ChatGPT 29.2 to 35.8. Spearman with analogy score: humans 62.5, best fine-tuned RoBERTa 25.0, FlanT5-xxl 4.7, ChatGPT 2.3. Annotator agreement Fleiss kappa 47 (entity) and 42 (relation) percent. Generation judged analogous: ChatGPT zero-shot 70.0, few-shot 78.3, fine-tuned FlanT5-xxl 72.5.
limits: Paper text and tables disagree slightly on the gap size. Models are better at generating analogies than at recognising them.
agent_relevance: Recognition of structural match is the weak step, generation is strong. Let the model propose analogues; let code or a second system score the mapping.

source: ARN: analogical reasoning on narratives (2023)
finding: Benchmark of narrative pairs with surface, relational and system mappings plus near and far settings. Models roughly halfway between chance and human in near analogy, and fall to 45.3 percent in the (far, far) condition where no surface cues help.
numbers: (far, far) score 45.3 percent; best model about halfway between random and human; SBERT similarity baseline also poor on far-far.
limits: Numbers from paper prose; only parts read. Exact human ceiling not noted.
agent_relevance: Confirms a systematicity gap: without shared surface, models do not reliably find the relational system. Argues for explicit structure extraction.

source: Das and Balke (2025) From prototypical to relational: how LLMs navigate complex analogies (INLG)
finding: Multi-answer analogy benchmark. Models such as GPT-4 do well on embedding and prototypicality measures but underperform on fine-grained relational mappings.
numbers: No numbers seen (search snippet only).
limits: Snippet only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Same gap in 2025: surface and prototype fit are good, fine-grained relations are not.

source: Weitekamp and MacLellan (2026) SMTB: fast structure-mapping with tight bounds
finding: New structure-mapping algorithm that maximises relational connectivity without privileging higher-order relations. 5 to 15 times faster than SME and finds about 50 percent more consistent correspondences in large nested domains. Shows cases where SME's higher-order bias fails.
numbers: Evaluated on 5,845 domain pairs from the SME corpus. Total time over corpus: SME 70.95 s; greedy SMTB 5.97 s; backtracking (width 3, depth 3, 27 arms) 30.99 s. Overall mapping-score gain over SME about 21.6 to 22.6 percent on SMTB objective; SME kernel-violation correspondences 1.24 to 1.78 percent overall (up to 10.58 percent in some domains). Large problems over 128 entities: 1.80x on SMTB objective, 1.52x on SME objective.
limits: Own authors' benchmark. Systematicity as an explicit preference is partly dropped, which questions the founding claim as a hard rule. Flat first-order domains give SME no higher-order signal.
agent_relevance: A fast open code library (Cognitive Rule Engine, Python over C++) exists for O7 mapping scored by code. Suggests scoring by connectivity, not just higher-order depth.

source: Crouse, Nakos, Abdelaziz, Forbus (2020) Neural analogical matching (AMN)
finding: A graph neural network trained on 100,000 purely synthetic analogies learned to produce structure-mapping-style matches on unseen real analogy corpora, reaching structural scores 95 to 104 percent of SME's.
numbers: Trained on 100,000 synthetic examples; tested on SME corpus domains and 1,000 synthetic examples. Structural score 95-104 percent of SME. Candidate-inference prediction also evaluated.
limits: Matches SME, so inherits SME's systematicity preference; no check against human data.
agent_relevance: A learned scorer can approximate SME cheaply, but code SME already exists, so a learned scorer adds little for O7.

source: Gentner and Forbus (2025) Structure-mapping engine review (Current Directions)
finding: Review says SME, created in 1986, is still used alone and inside CogSketch and Companion, and proposes these models as a technology for AI. A search found no SME plus LLM hybrid from the Forbus group.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Search snippet only, not opened.
agent_relevance: Cognitive-systems and LLM sides have not been merged publicly; an LLM extracts relations, SME maps hybrid would be new.

source: QRG Companion papers on analogical chaining (Blass and Forbus 2016)
finding: Companion architecture uses analogical chaining: several analogical retrievals elaborate a situation, giving plausible explanations and predictions. Predates LLMs and uses none.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Search snippet only, not opened.
agent_relevance: Chaining analogues to explain a case is an older agent-loop method for analogy; compare to O7 at impasses.

source: YARN: abstractions for narrative analogy, structural mapping with LLM-derived abstractions (2026)
finding: Modular pipeline: an LLM splits narratives into units, abstracts each unit at one of four levels, then a mapping component aligns elements across the stories. Abstractions consistently improved results, competitive with or better than end-to-end LLM baselines. Remaining errors: wrong abstraction level, implicit causality.
numbers: Four abstraction levels. No accuracy figures on the abstract page (full paper not read).
limits: Abstract page only. Authorship not noted; check before citing.
agent_relevance: Closest published LLM-extracts-then-code-maps loop. It is the pattern O7 proposes. The open problem is choosing the abstraction level.

source: The curious case of analogies: analogical reasoning in LLMs, mechanistic (2025)
finding: Models encode the relation between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, but often fail to apply it to a new entity. Patching hidden states at critical tokens partly fixes the transfer. Successful analogies show strong structural alignment in representation; failures show degraded alignment.
numbers: Three findings. No percentages on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract page only; authors not verified.
agent_relevance: Failure is in the application step, after the relation is found. Supports a separate, checked transfer step in O7.

source: Donvito and Lieto (2026) Minimal Cognitive Grid ranking of analogy and metaphor models
finding: Scores SME, CogSketch, METCL and LLMs on a quantified cognitive-plausibility grid (functional/structural ratio, generality, performance match).
numbers: Three dimensions. Per-model scores not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read.
agent_relevance: Gives a framework for judging whether our O7 is a structure-mapping model or a language-model surface method.

source: Stevenson et al. (2024) Do LLMs solve verbal analogies like children do?
finding: Six Dutch LLMs solved children's A:B::C:? analogies at 7 to 11 year-old level, and their errors followed association (the strong distractor, like the C term) rather than relation, as children's do.
numbers: 14,006 children aged 7-12 solved 622 Dutch analogies. M-GPT worst, about 7-year-old level; XLM-V and GPT-3 best, slightly above 11-year-old level. With only the C term shown, GPT-3 got 33 percent of items and XLM-V 28 percent correct. In A:C::B:? form accuracy dropped but stayed above 20 percent chance. XLM-V's top wrong answer matched most children's in 33 percent of cases.
limits: Dutch, single relation, verbal. Some item filtering departed from preregistration (250 items).
agent_relevance: Model errors are associative. A mapping step must check the relation, not the nearest word.

source: Lewis and Mitchell 2024 counterfactual comprehension checks
finding: Models passed comprehension checks on the altered alphabets, yet still failed the analogies, so failure is not just misreading the setup.
numbers: Table 1 in the paper reports check accuracy per model and alphabet size; exact values not extracted.
limits: Table values unread.
agent_relevance: A failed analogy with a passed comprehension check is a clean diagnostic to include in agent tests.

source: Webb et al. (2024) method note on GPT-4 refusals
finding: GPT-4 sometimes refused or hedged on letter-string problems, saying the pattern was too uncertain. Responses were regenerated until an answer appeared.
numbers: Method note only.
limits: Procedure detail that may inflate scores.
agent_relevance: Models may decline when the mapping is underdetermined; the agent should treat that as a signal, not retry silently.
